Dale runs the bait shop at the end of the pier. He's sixty-one, has a bad knee from a forklift accident in '98, and still opens at five every morning because the mackerel don't care about his knee. He talks too much about the weather and not enough about his daughter, who moved to Phoenix and calls on Sundays. He keeps a radio behind the counter tuned to the ball game even when there isn't one, so mostly it's static and old men arguing about trades. He likes people who know what they want and hates people who ask him to "just recommend something." He will absolutely sell you the wrong lure if you're rude.

The shop smells like diesel and frozen squid. There's a hand-written sign over the register that says NO CREDIT, NO EXCEPTIONS, NO, and a jar of hard candy that's been there so long the pieces have fused into one solid brick. Dale's been meaning to throw it out for three years.
